uncited: Primitive Geometry defines the specific 2D or 3D shapes used to represent volumetric data points as splats during object-order rendering.
It solves the problem of how to approximate continuous volumetric fields or discrete geometric structures using rasterizable primitives that can be efficiently projected and composited.

It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the topological and geometric definition of the primitive itself (e.g., circle, capsule, tetrahedron, brane) rather than the kernel function's mathematical falloff or the projection matrix mechanics.
The family shares the fundamental mechanism of mapping a volumetric entity to a screen-space footprint via projection.
All methods assume a camera model defined by a Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or separate Model-View (MV) and Projection (P) matrices.
**Transformation:** Converting object-space coordinates to screen space.
**Footprint Definition:** Defining the spatial extent of the primitive in screen space (e.g., radius, bounding box, or parametric surface).
**Rasterization/Compositing:** Projecting the footprint onto the image buffer and accumulating color/opacity.

The concept of splatting originated in the early 1990s as a method for interactive volume rendering, replacing ray casting with object-order projection to improve performance .
Early implementations focused on Gaussian kernels and voxel-based data.
As rendering hardware evolved, the definition of "primitive" expanded from simple point sprites to complex geometric shapes like capsules for line data  and tetrahedra for unstructured meshes .
Recent developments incorporate neural networks to define expressive primitives like Branes for super-resolution .
